title: Thoughts on Rohatsu and the Condition of the Nation's Welfare
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating compassion and understanding in the face of challenges and conflicts, drawing on the Buddha's wisdom from the Pali Canon. Kanho Chris Burkhart encourages listeners to consider how their own experiences and values align with the Buddha's teachings, which prioritize peace and respect over division and aggression. By approaching problems with a calm and open mind, we can work towards growth and understanding rather than conflict and destruction.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma, [unclear: "Israeli"] met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept.
I vow to taste the truth of the [unclear: "tatakura's"] words.*
Good morning, and sorry for the slow start.
I am engaged in this war with my printer, and the printer is definitely winning, so I will need to read directly off my laptop.
Good morning, dear friends.
This is my last talk for this year, and I very much appreciate all of you hanging in there with me.
Thank you for being here today and sharing this morning. 2021: sometimes it felt so long, and now it is December, and I truly don't know where it went.
2022: I will dare to make some predictions.
Global warming will not disappear.
Political upset will not disappear.
COVID will not disappear.
Of course, as individuals we can swim against the streams, and like salmon we may be able to make it up river for a certain distance, and our effort can take us to a different place.
But still, we don't change the direction of the river, and we don't make the water run uphill.
But I want us not to become discouraged and do the easy thing.
What I am asking of all of us is to continue our practice.
Not to put on a bandaid or to fix something, but simply because this is who we are, and this is what we do.
The other point is that the question is not about swimming with or against the current, or just drifting along.
It is about taking the appropriate action at the right time, seeing beyond our conditioning and habit patterns.
Now that New Year's Eve is approaching quickly, there will be one more Zen life this year.
Jordan Bob Rose will be the speaker.
I look forward to his talk, because usually he does not engage our sense of hearing, but our senses of tasting and smelling to spread the Dharma.
Bob has been our Tenzo for more than five years now, and we are all very happy with his cooking and very grateful to Bob and his generous nature.
Usually, Red Cedar has a great celebration on New Year's Eve.
To ring out the old year and ring in the new, we have 108 strikes of our big [unclear: "ringgong"] bell.
And we light a fire and we send our innermost thoughts and wishes and regrets to the heavens in smoke.
This year, it will be quiet.
We're taking a break during the last week of December.
So our first community event will be Zen life on January 2, and [unclear: "no one"] Tim Burnett will be the speaker.
Also, Zen life will remain online in 2022, mostly due to the number of guest speakers who are not local.
And now a heads up for our local folks, even though I'm quite sure you all know all about it.
Our in-person program will change in two respects in the new year.
Number one, we will be moving from the Shambhala Center on Meridian to the Unitarian Church on Ellsworth.
Number two, we will shift our evening practice from Wednesdays to Thursdays.
Also, our practice period will begin in January.
Seiu Hannah Sullivan will serve as Shuso, the head student, and she will be talking about the Diamond Sutra.
Her teacher, Sokaku Cathy Fisher, will be here for the opening and closing events of the practice period, and also supporting Hannah in her journey as Shuso.
If you wish to participate, please sign up online.
Also, if you are interested, you can sign up for a practice partner, which is actually kind of fun.
I am so happy that we will be meeting in person again.
I was touched by how intimate the Rohatsu sesshin felt, to actually sit with living beings without a screen in between.
Rohatsu celebrates the Great Awakening, the transformation of Siddhartha Gautama into the Buddha.
This is the core of the story.
Finally, Siddhartha came to a quiet place near the river and sat down under a huge tree.
He settled down with a simple yet unshakable vow to stay still until he realized the truth.
Because of that diamond-sharp, solid, and clear commitment, the place he did zazen is called the indestructible seat.
It is the Bodhi Seat, the seat of enlightenment, the same seat you are sitting on, that anybody doing zazen is sitting on.
When the morning star appeared, he was suddenly enlightened and spoke the words, "I and all sentient beings on earth together attain enlightenment at the same time."
This, of course, is our austere Zen version of the event.
According to the Theravadan tradition, he uttered the following words:
*Through the round of many births I roamed, without reward, without rest, seeking the house-builder.
Painful is birth, again and again.
House-builder, you are seen.
You will not build a house again.
All your raft is broken, the [unclear: "rich pole"] destroyed.
Gone to the unformed, the mind has come to the end of craving.*
That is the message of awakening that we heard during [unclear: "Yubo Hatsu"].
Now, looking ahead, looking at 2022, a different passage from the Pali Canon came up for me, and it refused to be put aside.
I actually had planned on a very different talk, but what can I say?
So what I will talk about instead are the conditions of the nation's welfare.
The internet has its blessings and curses.

Perhaps we have become so comfortable with our central heating and air conditioning, with grocery stores and SUVs, that the current social instability and the decline of democracy feel like personal attacks.
Sometimes it is hard to realize that in the middle of this mess, our lives are not bad at all.
At the same time, I feel that social engagement is essential to create change, because it appears that recurring social unrest is built into humanity.
It was like this when Shunryu Suzuki came to America.
Japan was not a quiet place.
It happened in Dogen's time.
It happened in China and Japan to our Buddhist ancestors.
And it happened in the Buddha's time.
That war between the Vajis and the kingdom of Magadha was brewing.
So please have patience with me, because I'm a bit of a geek.
When I prepare for a talk, I read and study and explore different things.
I found some information on Wikipedia about the Buddha's home country, Magadha, that I found absolutely fascinating.
It appears that the culture of Magadha was in fundamental ways different from the kingdoms of the Indo-Aryans.
Magadha was considered a hostile tribe, living and threatening the borders of Vedic India.
There is an argument for a cultural area termed Greater Magadha, and it is roughly the geographical area in which the Buddha lived and taught.

Suggestive of this distinction, in some Vedic and post-Vedic rituals, a Magadha man represents the canonical non-Vedic barbarian, the Magadha standing in for the presence of any and all non-Vedic peoples or the ritually impure.
I thought that was really fascinating.
I would also like to structure the rest of the talk a little bit differently from what I usually do.
I will be reading the opening of the Maha Paranibbana Sutta, The Last Days of the Buddha.
In that passage, the Buddha talks about the strength and the welfare of a nation.
This is the only writing about politics that I've found in all of the Pali Canon, which is the oldest writings in our tradition.
I hope that the seven points that the Buddha makes can inspire a conversation about maybe what is the same, what is different, or how you feel about those points that the Buddha made.
And I will be sharing the pith points at the end of the conversation, so you don't need to write it down or memorize it.
First, a little bit of background on the actors in the scene that is about to unfold.
We are, of course, familiar with the Buddha and Ananda.
They both came from the kingdom of Magadha.
Achatasatu is the current king of Magadha.
His father, Achatasatu's father, was King Bimbisara, who was a good friend of the Buddha.
Footnote: rumor has it that Achatasatu murdered his father, Bimbisara, to gain the throne.
To the footnote, he was in turn apparently murdered by his own son.
The next person in the scene is Vasakara.
He is a Brahmin and Achatasatu's chief minister.
The Vajji Confederacy and the kingdom of Magadha are neighbors.
All right, the stage is set.
Vasakara, who is Achatasatu's chief minister, approaches the Buddha.
*He approached the Blessed One on foot.
After exchanging courteous greetings with the Blessed One, together with many pleasant words, he sat down at one side and addressed the Blessed One thus.*
*Venerable Gautama, Achatasatu, the king of Magadha, pays homage at the feet of the Venerable Gautama and wishes him good health, strength, ease, vigor, and comfort.
He desires to wage war against the Vajjis, and he has spoken in this fashion.
These Vajjis, powerful and glorious as they are, I shall annihilate them.
I shall make them perish.
I shall utterly destroy them.*
Well, you may wonder if the Buddha will reply, "Ah, don't do this.
War is not good for beings.
And as a good Buddhist, we don't do war.
I'm a peace-bringer," he might have said.
"Another solution should be found," he might have said.
But perhaps the World Honored One accepted that war was a reality in his time and place.
Maybe he knew that war will happen no matter what he says.
So what the Buddha said was this.
*At that time, the Venerable Ananda was standing behind the Blessed One fanning him, and the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ananda thus.
What have you heard, Ananda?
Do the Vajjis have frequent gatherings, and are their meetings well attended?
I have heard, Lord, that this is so.*
The Buddha again:
*So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.*
*What have you heard, Ananda?
Do the Vajjis assemble and disperse peacefully and attend to their affairs in concord?
I have heard, Lord, that they do.*
And the Buddha again:
*So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.*
*What have you heard, Ananda?
Do the Vajjis neither enact new decrees nor abolish existing ones, but proceed in accordance with the ancient constitutions?
I have heard, Lord, that they do.*
And the Buddha again:
*So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.*
*What have you heard, Ananda?
Do the Vajjis show respect, honor, esteem, and veneration towards their elders, and think it worthwhile to listen to them?
I have heard, Lord, that they do.*
*So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.*
*What have you heard, Ananda?
Do the Vajjis refrain from abducting women and maidens of good families, and from detaining them?
I have heard, Lord, that they refrain from doing so.*
A little side note here.
A different translation: I don't have the interpretation whether the Vajjis force women into marriages against their will.
So I do not know what the better translation is.
*So do the Vajjis refrain from abducting women and maidens of good families, and from detaining them?
I have heard, Lord, that they refrain from doing so.*
*So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.*
*What have you heard, Ananda?

Do the Vajjis show respect, honor, esteem, and veneration towards their shrines, both those within the city and those outside it, and do not deprive them of the due offerings as given or made to them formerly?*
And Ananda replied:
*I have heard, Lord, that they do venerate their shrines and that they do not deprive them of their offerings.*
*So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.*
*What have you heard, Ananda?
Do the Vajjis duly protect and guard the Arahats so that those who have not come to the [unclear: "realm"] yet might do so, and those who have already come might live in peace?
I have heard, Lord, that they do.*
*So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.*
*And the Blessed One addressed the Brahmin Vasakara in these words.
So long, Brahmin, as these seven conditions leading to a nation's welfare endure among the Vajjis and the Vajjis are known for it, their growth is to be expected, not their decline.*
*Thereupon, the Brahmin Vasakara spoke thus to the Blessed One.
No harm indeed can be done to the Vajjis in battle by Magadha's King Achadasattu, except through treachery or discord.
Well then, Venerable Gautama, we will take our leave, for we have much to perform, much work to do.
Do as now seems fit to you, Brahmin.
And the Brahmin Vasakara, the Chief Minister of Magadha, approving of the Blessed One's words and delighted by them, rose from his seat and departed.*
It is very interesting that both Buddhist and Chinese traditional scriptures recall this war, although the storylines are quite different.
You can take your pick as the cause of the war between the output of a shared diamond mine or the personal greed of the Magadha royal household.
And in the end, the kingdom of Magadha won the war.
And how was it done?
Achadasattu sent his Chief Minister Vasakara to infiltrate the Vajji Confederacy.
Probably he was not alone, but he's the only one mentioned.
He caused political unrest.
He probably lied.
There was probably sabotage.
All that resulted in the destruction of the altars and the destruction of the civil society.
Within three years, Vasakara had sown enough discord that the seven conditions leading to a nation's welfare and to the unity of the Vajjis were destroyed.
*An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect Dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.*
I am sorry, I'm drawing an absolute blank.
Achadas, could you please chant the closing?
*To see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow...*
Oh, we started wrong.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of the Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
